subject: religious-studies
title: Trinity and Incarnation
welcome_lead: Enter the ecumenical councils of the patristic age where the Church hammered out its doctrines of the triune God and the incarnate Word.
meta_desc: A-Level AQA Religious Studies adventure on the Trinity and Incarnation: Nicaea, Chalcedon, and the contributions of Augustine and Aquinas.
final_note: You have traced how the Church confessed one God in three persons and one Christ in two natures.

concepts.def: Greek for 'of the same substance'; the Nicene term affirming the Son's full divinity with the Father.
Greek term meaning 'person' or 'subsistence', used of the three persons of the Trinity.
The mutual indwelling and interpenetration of the three divine persons.
The union of divine and human natures in the one person of Christ, defined at Chalcedon (451).
The Latin clause 'and from the Son', added to the Nicene Creed and disputed by Eastern Christianity.
The self-emptying of the Son in the incarnation, drawn from Philippians 2:7.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Council of Nicaea (325) confessed the Son as homoousios with the Father against Arius, who held the Son was a creature. Constantinople I (381) completed trinitarian doctrine by affirming the divinity of the Holy Spirit, who 'proceeds from the Father' and is 'worshipped and glorified' with the Father and Son. The Cappadocian Fathers (Basil, the two Gregorys) gave the formula: one ousia, three hypostases.

Against Apollinarianism (Christ lacks a human mind), Nestorianism (two persons) and Eutychianism (one mixed nature), the Council of Chalcedon (451) defined Christ as 'truly God and truly man... in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation', united in one person and hypostasis.

walkthroughs.h2: Augustine and Aquinas on the Trinity
walkthroughs.body_html: Augustine, in De Trinitate, develops psychological analogies (memory, understanding, will) for the inner life of God. Aquinas, in Summa Theologiae I, QQ.27-43, distinguishes the divine persons by their relations of origin: paternity, filiation, and spiration. Both stress that the external works of the Trinity are undivided (opera ad extra sunt indivisa).
